items.title: j'ai ce besoin vital, insatiable, d'étancher ma curiosité
items.summary: Alors oui, je l'ai déjà dit dans l'un de mes premiers articles,…
items.content_html:
Alors oui, je l'ai déjà dit dans l'un de mes premiers articles, mais voilà: il semble que mon unique ambition ces derniers temps est celle qui relève de mon capital culturel. Malheureusement (c'est un constat plus qu'un regret), ma personnalité fait que je vire rapidement vers l'obsession plutôt que de me contenter d'une jolie petite information toute fraîche lue dans le dernier article de Vanessa Friedman sur le style vestimentaire de Mark Zuckerberg, que je pourrais sans doute partager avec une… bon, on va dire quelqu'un… mais non.

 
En quelques secondes, j'ai 57 onglets ouverts : loro piana vicuña 2 000 hectares au pérou mais qui s'occupe d'eux, priscilla chan medical school residency where, essilorluxottica family day, is Ana Khouri jewelry designer lebanese, mark zuckerberg front row prada fashion industry backlash, etc. etc.
 
Et puis il ne faut pas oublier les notes dans mon 5e Moleskine de l'année, les pages Notion où je me répète sans cesse par peur d'oublier l'information, les méga-threads sur Notes, les post-it sur le miroir du lavabo ou sur le capot du Mac, ou pire : les interminables diapositives Google Slides, où chaque présentation est un "dossier" dédié à une thématique spécifique (Fashion Dossier, Gastronomy Dossier, Design Dossier, Quotes Dossier), où chaque image doit être soigneusement sélectionnée pour matcher l'esthétique que j'ai en tête (exemple : puisque la lettre "t" est la plus récurrente dans tout le texte et qu'il n'y a pas beaucoup de "l", alors il faut que visuellement ça paraisse rose framboise. wtf mais c'est vrai), où chaque interligne est identique, où chaque usage du gras, de l'italique, ou du souligné est conforme à mon code typographique du moment…

 
I won't bore you with every single detail of the inner workings of my mind, but you get the gist.
 
Petite pause avant de vraiment partir en vrille.
 

On continue. 

J'ai euh, bon on va le dire : j'ai un peu le cul entre deux chaises. Je m'engage dans un parcours évidemment long et exigeant (un peu trop tourné vers la science PURE à mon goût)… vous l'aurez deviné, c'est la médecine. Ceux qui me connaissent savent que depuis ce fameux épisode de C'est pas sorcier sur le système digestif en CM1 j'ai tracé tout mon parcours en termes d'études, et de carrière, et de projets… et même de garde-robe. Je tiens tout de même à préciser que les idées que j'avais, disons jusqu'au lycée, étaient principalement décidées après avoir googlé : "best medical school in the world", "best hospital in the world", "highest paid doctor specialty", "Upper East Side mom outfits" blablabla. 

Dieu merci, la situation géopolitique envenimée par les décisions d'un certain monsieur blond (enfin, fluo ou jsp) au teint abricot a fait du Canada mon nouveau projet de vie. 

Mais attention, j'ai très vite compris que ça ne rigolait pas trop avec les "1st Year Life Sciences UofT student, hoping to pursue a triple specialist in neuroscience, immunology and physiology, aspiring neurosurgeon, SickKids volunteer, lifeguard… Trinity College" sur LinkedIn. 

Pre-med students are little snakes. Pas tous évidemment, mais un peu oui. Un peu tous.

En plus de m'être fait harceler par les annonces Wizeprep: Crush Your MCAT Exam, ELITE 515+ Tutoring ($7,199 CAD btw) placardées sur chaque mur du campus (même aux toilettes, bruh), de me faire bombarder d'événements de clubs "How to find research opportunities as a 1st year student!" à chaque fois que j'ouvrais insta (je me suis lassée à une vitesse record des Cheese Pizzas de chez Pizza Pizza et des douzaines de boîtes de Timbits), où c'était toujours le même contenu répété en boucle (how to land a lab position, cold emailing, etc. etc.), et pas mal de rencontres, notamment avec ce mec d'origine perse à 11 h du soir à Graham Library qui m'a pratiquement dit de foutre le camp d'ici et de retourner en Europe dans n'importe quelle fac de médecine au lieu de me retrouver dans la même position que lui : avoir fini son bachelor à Toronto, puis avoir tout repris à zéro à la fac de médecine en Allemagne, puis avoir obtenu sa résidence au Canada, et maintenant réviser pour passer son examen et transférer aux États-Unis… inutile de préciser que mon enthousiasme de 2017 en a pris un sacré coup.

They do everything to distract you from your GPA: taking on all those volunteering positions where all you do is stand in a dark lab doing the lowest-level grunt work for 10 to 15 hours a week, joining all those random clubs, campaigning to be elected as Junior Representative of a club that meets twice a semester, all just to write a three-sentence bullet point on your OMSAS application.

Ok, obviously, on rencontre de tout à l'université. Et franchement, ce ne sont pas mes compétences académiques qui me préoccupent le plus dans toute cette histoire. Et who's to say if someone was not able to do it, you can't do it? Guys, don't let negative people get to you. Mais je pense que c'est tout simplement une multitude de choses qui a fait que j'ai changé d'elevator pitch quand on me pose la question de ce que je veux faire plus tard. Surtout. Avec. D'autres. Étudiants.

Alors oui, je pense peut-être me spécialiser en Human Biology, jsp, et après on va voir. Médecine ? Ah ouais peut-être. Un PhD, un MPH, ou alors full-time dog walker (je hais les chiens, mais l'air frais, tu vois). Bah oui, je suis sérieuse. Sinon, un kiosque de hot-dogs devant Robarts, histoire de rester sur le campus. Ou un master en biostatistiques. Idk, à voir. Et pire des cas j'ouvrirai mon épicerie à la belle vie à Rabat. C'est où Rabat ? C'est au Maroc. T'inquiète, c'est pas au programme du MCAT.

Ouais, j'aime bien garder mes options ouvertes.

Je ne voulais surtout pas être associée aux (no shade) fanatiques des lymphocytes T auxiliaires folliculaires de type 1. 

I think this was the turning point that reallyyyyy made me YEARN to show another side of myself, and it ended up revealing what I am truly looking for (ok cringe, but seriously). 

J'ai toujours été attirée par le côté humain de la médecine, c'est-à-dire (à l'époque) les liens qu'ont différentes cultures avec le monde de la santé. Ce n'est qu'après mes cours d'anthropologie médicale à la fac que je me suis rendu compte à quel point c'est tellement plus vaste, et en même temps tellement ancré dans notre quotidien.

Tout ce que je viens d'écrire m'amène à mes prochains propos, mais je tenais à expliquer que, malgré le fait qu'en surface mes intérêts n'aient aucun lien avec celui de la science, de la médecine, ou de la santé, je pense sincèrement qu'ils ne peuvent que me servir. Parce qu'un médecin anthropologue cultivé et instruit, bah il n'y a pas mieux, quoi.

what the pope has for breakfast 

blue mountain school london

watch the canadian parliament live → house of commons sitting calendar (green = sitting day) if the mps are working in ottawa + check the hour-by-hour written schedule of what bills are being debated

andrée putman interior design of the concorde cabin

work is not 9 to 5 anymore: truck drivers, uber eats, late-night restaurants → gyms open 24h

institut supérieur international du parfum, de la cosmétique et de l'aromatique alimentaire (founded by guerlain)

why do so many black americans enlist in the military (when they make up a lower share of us civilian population)

instinct ai: invite-only personal ai agent gone viral

hospital architecture

ferragamo cara medium shoulder bag (there's even an exotic eel skin leather option, shiny)

sarah sitkin hyper realistic statues *tw

cfa exam (post on the hypocrisy of investment bankers in the neoliberal capitalist market x canadian pension funds coming soon)

margiela numeric coding

redundant staff = employee jobs no longer needed by company (duplicate roles example companies merge 2 hrs, job replaced by tech/automation)

axon cameras replacing flock cameras

masters of our destiny (oufff trop fort Carbon Tax Carney!) liberals' budget for 2026 (I AM LITERALLY CAPABLE OF READING EVERY SINGLE PAGE OF THAT 532-PAGE PDF AS IF MY LIFE DEPENDED ON IT, please send help)

techno-ravers groups berlin (head-to-toe black gear, oversized puffers, and stomper boots)

guéridon table jean prouvé

rick owens black temple beatle bozo tractor boots

chanterelle mushrooms dish

tissu brocard

polyester underwear infertility (cotton or organic cotton instead)

high quality soy sauce should form a thick layer of fine bubbles and foam at the top when shaken

phoebe philo is cheaper in europe

Je suis littéralement en train de compléter le certificat LVMH en parallèle avec mes cours de biochimie / génétique / statistiques.

Et encore ça c'est en temps normal.

Faut MÊME pas qu'on reparle de ces dernières semaines de septembre : La Fashion Week. Tout ce temps que j'ai passé sur Vogue Runway à screenshotter les détails des looks, à regarder les stories de tous ces fashion editors / journalists sur insta to keep track of what new pop-up is taking place or who's at the show afterparty or what was the menu at the private dinner, les vlogs behind the scenes de Loïc Prigent, et évidemment mes podcasts, mes magnum opus : brendawareness et Fashion People de Lauren Sherman.

Au-delà de la mode, j'ai carrément un créneau bloqué le matin consacré uniquement à mes newsletters (heavily inspired by Anna Wintour's morning routine of catching up on the news) : normalement je lis The Morning du New York Times (tho this shit is SO biased it makes me want to wash my eyes with bleach), le podcast CBC World Report, et je lis les titres de Al Jazeera.

Et pour le reste de la journée, je pioche un peu partout :

Déjà, toutes les news canadiennes : The Globe and Mail, CBC, Toronto Star, The Local, The Breach.

For fashion: Vogue (for EIC newsletters, Chloe Malle's is way better imo than Claire Thomson-Jonville's, which is just her talking about how much she loves working out and knee-high boots), Back Row, 1 Granary (it's on Substack, and there's barely any free stuff left), je suis aussi abonnée aux lookbooks de Byronesque, et Miss Tweed (tho not sure how reliable her reporting is after the whole LVMH / Hedi thing).

Art and design: Architectural Digest, Artsy, Art21.

Then the pop culture stuff: Celebrity Intelligence, et j'aime bien, une fois par mois, ouvrir Hello! Magazine sur navigateur to see what new junk is out there.

Though I might not be subscribed to them, I also open / lis les titres de Rest of World (quick overview what's going on in the tiers monde), Monocle (for aesthetic delusional positivity), et IRMA's World (travel inspo, delusional on MY part this time).

I am not much of a Substack user tbh. The layout of the app bothers me A LOT. I still literally watched every freaking YouTube Shorts "tutorial" on what every single button does (God forbid when I get a car, imma need to find a way to resist the compulsion to read the entire manual to learn what every single button is for and Google hidden features on the display screen, it's never-ending; also THANK GOD I AM NOT A PILOT, I MEAN WHAT WOULD MY LIFE EVEN LOOK LIKE??????).

 
 
 

I watch a lot of documentaries on Kanopy or Enquête Exclusive or ARTE before bed, and if I am feeling preoccupied with Canadian stuff (and feel the civic duty to act as an informed citizen of democracy), I put on Radio-Canada Info or The Fifth Estate for .

One of my strict rules regarding consumption (I'm talking money consumerism cuz those subscriptions don't come in cheap) is: NO LIMIT FOR BOOKS. Literally. I will never, ever let myself feel bad about buying a book or a magazine. Obviously, I am not dumb enough to get them from those little wine bar concept stores with the "staff selection" or the Miu Miu oval glasses "Literary Girlies" neighborhood book club curated selection (I am physically cringing typing this), where each book costs $45 CAD instead of $20 CAD on Amazon (I do not order books from Amazon either, fyi). I find good deals elsewhere. There are so many places that offer free used books, so my finances can stay safe.
 
The reason for this rule is that books, or PRINT things in general (I feel very desolate when I say this) will DISAPPEAR VERY SOON. Literally, I don't know why people ARE NOT TALKING ABOUT the fact that AI companies are buying, then scanning, then feeding books to their grotesque machines only to DESTROY THEM. I'M TALKING RARE, LIMITED-EDITION BOOKS. HELLOOOO?????? 

Je suis consciente que ça devient trop long là, mais contenu demeure encore très superficiel. Je tiens à mentionner que l'essentiel pour le capital culturel, c'est tout ce qui relève des vraies expériences. Et c'est selon moi la chose indispensable pour vraiment, vraiment devenir cultivée. Parce que oui, ok, les médias, les magazines, les livres, c'est sympa et tout, mais tu restes chez toi quoi.

Il faut sortir, ouvrir les yeux, regarder les chaussures des gens, les stickers sur la coque de leur ordi, leur commande de café, leurs ongles (rongés, vernis écaillé ou manucure russe parfaite, acryliques Hello Kitty chez nos amis de l'Extrême-Orient), la coupe de leur manteau, leur fond d'écran, ce qu'ils bouffent, le ton de leur voix.

Le moment préféré de ma journée, c'est quand je sors vers 7 h du mat avec mon café pour voir les gens préparer leur petit-déjeuner, puis les parents sortir avec leurs gosses à l'arrière du vélo, et les écoliers et écolières en jupe d'uniforme malgré le froid.

Un de mes prochains articles portera sur Toronto et sur comment j'essaie de chaparder chaque petit détail pour enrichir mon capital culturel, que ce soit en assistant aux débats municipaux (et en passant à la télé en live) ou en passant l'après-midi à regarder my giant friend, Draped Seated Woman, à l'AGO.

Disclaimer : cet article n'est en AUCUN CAS un guide d'organisation. Ceci n'est PAS de l'organisation. J'écrirai bientôt un énorme article sur le sujet, et vous verrez que mon organisation est bien, bien, bien meilleure que ma façon de penser. En fait, je crois même que c'est ma plus grande fierté

I'm like an antennae, you know, like a building with an antennae that captures everything, I want to know everything. 

Karl Lagerfeld

items.title: designer, consumer dumber
items.summary: In the spirit of fashion week (and CFDA heads wrestling PETA protesters)…
items.content_html:
In the spirit of fashion week (and CFDA heads wrestling PETA protesters) let's talk about what exactly we're buying when we buy fashion. So here is my unhinged rant on why we’re so easily convinced that expensive equals good, and how brands are blatantly profiting from it.

For preface: I don't particularly like the word "luxury." It is very overused. I also hate using the word "chic." Like, it's just not chic to say something is chic in writing. Though, I do think it’s fine in a conversation, and it’s even better when you simply think it. 

Anyways, the point is: knowing fashion is kind of (actually, it IS) cultural capital.

Veblen Economics 101

Let's start with some interesting context about aspirational marketing. Chanel, Dior, Rolex, all of these brands put up huge billboards at random bus stations in front of people who have absolutely no intention/budget to buy the product being advertised.

But… public recognition creates status. So when everyone knows that a logo costs an obscene amount of money, the logo becomes a dream. Fortunately for capitalism, it wins. Enter the $120 eau de parfum, the ultimate "accessible luxury" gateway. You might NOT walk out with a Chanel flap bag, but you still can grab a small tangible piece of the illusion at an airport duty-free!

Moving on to the ridiculous economics of Veblen goods. A Veblen good is a product for which demand can increase as its price increases because the price itself contributes to the item's desirability. Example: if the price of milk goes up, I am not going to think, wow, what an exciting status symbol, let me buy three. But if the price of a Chanel flap bag doubles, everyone knows it's even MORE exclusive, so the price becomes part of the product (hope I'm making sense). 

Looking back on my wonderful 6 to 9 PM evenings in PSY100, this is actually a prime example of a price-quality heuristic: the brain shortcut that something expensive must be better (quite convenient for the people selling expensive things, huh?). But as we will get into, expensive very often does NOT equal exceptional. 

Fabriqué Where?

First, the label.

"Made in Italy." "Made in France." Italy. France. Paris. Florence. The atelier. The little French flag…

There is a loophole-ish EU rule called the "last substantial transformation" that brands love.

I know it’s much more complicated than "finish it in France and slap on the label." But to simplify things (and get you to visualize the whole ordeal) some brands manufacture almost an entire product in low-wage countries, then add the final part (like a zipper or a button) in Europe. This is how you get a designer bag, possibly produced in China, but with a FABRIQUÉ EN FRANCE label!

Now, now. If you're paying for geography, might as well pay for exclusivity (cough, cough... supply control) too.

Lots of fashion brands have famously destroyed their unsold stock instead of discounting it/selling off excess. Burberry made headlines back in 2018 when it announced it was ending the practice of destroying unsaleable products (honestly, wouldn't be surprised if other major fashion houses are still doing something similar today). I mean, you have to make the product desirable. If everyone has it, you've got problems.

These brands did start to use AI, though, to make production volumes more exact. Interesting uses of AI, no? From building ballistic weapons to world cup football analytics to reducing the number of unsold Burberry trenches that would otherwise get torched. Versatile, to say the least.

The Death of Personal Taste

In terms of the boutiques/actual retail spaces…

I love curation. I love a buyer who actually has taste. Fashion buyers at major multi-brand retailers have, in many ways, a curatorial role, and I find that extremely impressive. Dover Street Market, Neiman Marcus, Bergdorf Goodman, whatever the particular store, isn't it interesting when someone who's looked at thousands of things, gone through thousands of line sheets, and decided that THESE are the things worth putting in front of you?

Unfortunately, today almost every luxury store carries its own copied version of the designer bag next door (think the Bottega intrecciato). Everything looks the same because every company/brand is responding to the same collected data! The algorithm feeds our need to hyper-share or show off and interestingly it turns out that most people actually LIKE being marketed to. People like being told what to wear and how to wear because the internet ruined the difference between your own taste and collectively assigned taste. 

So yes, fashion today (at least the version of fashion that is presented to most of us) is overwhelmingly mass-produced. There’s always going to be another version later. A better version. A cheaper version. A version with a slightly different pocket. A version that becomes the new "it" bag simply because the old one got overexposed and turned cringe.

Les Fashions Débarquent à Paris

We like to imagine fashion week as this cool fun event where the world's illustrious celebrities and most important creative people gather in black clothing and sit front row to criticize garments. Which, to be fair, does happen. But fashion is also a business, and the shows ultimately have to sell fashion too, especially to the clients and VICs who spend enormous amounts of money. There are estimated to be around 4,000 active haute couture clients worldwide (side note: haute couture ≠ ready-to-wear), while British Vogue has cited estimates that the top 2% of luxury customers can account for around 40% of luxury sales globally. I'm just gonna let that PSY201 statistical level of understanding unravel in my mind like a loose thread on a fast-fashion sweater while I stare blankly into the Zoom camera…

Fashion and art obviously share a clientèle. I won't get into the debate about whether fashion is art or design because frankly I have places to be and amino acid structures to learn, but money is always connected.

I am still investigating the Toronto VIC scene so I don’t feel very qualified to give you THAT full ethnographic report yet, but the Mink Mile, I personally find a bit tacky/performative. This is the supposedly high-end commercial strip of Bloor Street that people sometimes describe as Toronto's equivalent of Fifth Avenue or Rodeo Drive. There are luxury flagships (of course with security guards standing behind the glass looking like they’re protecting the Crown Jewels instead of a leather handbag) plus Holt Renfrew, Harry Rosen, and then my personal favorite, Winners, where I found an amazing Sandro blouse for about a fifth of the retail price not that long ago.

Anyway.

Go down the Reddit rabbit hole and you'll find entire communities discussing counterfeit luxury goods, factories, materials, stitching, hardware, packaging… with subreddits like r/RealRepLadies. Boy, will the internet ever cease to amaze me? You can find videos and discussions about underground factories and occasionally, the horrifying possibility that the line between authentic and fake is incredibly thin, much thinner than the marketing would like you to believe. Some brands (Moncler, Salvatore Ferragamo, Chloé) have responded with new authentication technologies, though.

Importantly, let’s remember that somewhere in the background, Arnault and Pinault are getting richer. So, as nice as the idea of romanticizing fashion sounds, it's impossible to ignore that it IS an industry. There are shareholders and conglomerates and margins and targets and expansion plans and supply chains and clients and sales figures…

Read the Tag, Please

I went to Santa Eulalia in Barcelona recently. I tried to act in the unfazed poised manner of a Gazelle de Waller, but my eyes kept widening involuntarily at the AUDACITY of the price tags.

A viscose-polyester blend Courrèges knit cardigan for €750? 

EXCUZE me?

Take The Row gala pants as another example (made of 69% triacetate and 31% polyester, retailing for €1,180). The Row and Toteme are, objectively, quite boring to me, but they have found an extremely effective way to convince people that boring is the result of quality, restraint, taste, and therefore worth several hundred or several thousand dollars.

Maybe the quality is actually amazing. How would I know?

Bref, paying more attention to what is actually in the clothes is quite important if you are going to spend money on your wardrobe (I recommend a one-time Jennifer Wang doomscroll to cure the delusions).

First, inspect the stitching and make sure it's uniform and straight. Channel your inner Anna Wintour looking for an excuse to fire someone. Turn the garment inside out, gently, and look at the seams. Check for reinforcement around stress points such as pockets and buttonholes. Look at the pattern alignment, especially with something like tweed (it’s extremely obvious if the pattern doesn’t continue properly across a seam).

Button-down shirts should have a yoke.

Check the lining (it definitely should NOT look like someone gave up halfway through the inside because, apparently, nobody will see it).

Look at the buttons. Real buttons should feel cold on the cheek.

With denim, check the selvedge. Look at the inside outseam of the jean leg.

Check the draping on the hanger. Pay attention to weight. And, obviously, you need to be able to walk in the garment because, frankly, I will not care about how beautiful your trousers are if you look like you've been medically immobilized from the knees down.

Look for loose threads and pilling. Check the zippers. 

In terms of fabric composition…

You've got synthetic fibers: polyester, nylon, elastane, acrylic. Polyester does not wrinkle easily. Elastane is kind of mandatory in leggings and other types of garments.

Then, semi-synthetic fibers such as viscose, modal and lyocell. These are made from cellulose-based material. Their environmental impact depends on the raw material and manufacturing process.

Best for last: natural fibers. Cotton. Silk. Wool. Hemp. Cashmere. Linen. Alpaca. Mohair (which comes from the Angora goat not the Angora rabbit). Cotton and linen together, for example, can make a very breathable summer fabric.

For leather, it’s a tad more complicated. Exotic skins such as python, caiman, ostrich, stingray and crocodile are usually sourced from animals specifically raised or harvested for their skins. But calfskin and other cattle leather are generally a byproduct of the meat industry.

Wear It Again

I personally think leather goods that develop a thick patina are beautiful. Even Miuccia Prada seems to understand the beauty of ugly, froissé, worn-in things. 

I am definitely putting words into her mouth now, but think of the actual Miu Miu girl archetype (not the influencer activation hobo bag version of it). 

There is something much more interesting about a garment that looks like it has lived.

Which is also why I think everyone should repeat outfits.

Outfit repeating is normal. It's sustainable. It's creative. 

Honestly, everyone should have a uniform.

Buy colors that work on you instead of whatever color happens to be trending for the next six weeks. 

Research what you're wearing. 

Learn why the garment is constructed the way it is. 

If you're a woman, check whether your pockets are shallow. Unfortunately, most women's pockets continue to barely house a single tube of ChapStick.

The Case for Vintage

Some people literally make a living sourcing wardrobes for clients (which I also find very impressive). 

Vestiaire Collective can be fantastic if you're in Europe, although in Canada I would avoid the heart-wrenching customs fees and international shipping whenever possible. The RealReal is also another story if you're outside the US.

There's a whole Toronto vintage and consignment world though. But that deserves its own post.

For outlets, if you're shopping at Winners or Marshalls, look at the single digit printed right next to the little square box on the price tag. Brands like Calvin Klein, Michael Kors, Tommy Hilfiger, Steve Madden, Kate Spade make cheaper clothes specifically to sell at these stores. Code 1 means the item was cheaply made just for Winners, while Code 2 (and 7) means it's a real department store designer item left over.

Contemplations…

Which brings me to my main takeaway:

BUY ONCE, BUY RIGHT.

Le bon marché coûte cher, mais l'argent ne fait pas le bonheur.

And before anyone accuses me of turning into some total fabric snob, I'm sure half my closet is recycled polyester. I'm not pretending I’ve never bought synthetic clothes. Honestly, I only got interested in fabrics and the business side of fashion because I realized how little I actually knew about what I was buying.

You do not have to buy everything.

You do not have to own the "best" version.

You do not even have to care about designer clothing.

You just have to come to terms with the fact that very often the IDEA of owning an item is much more exciting than actually owning it.

This is why fashion is really interesting to me.

I genuinely love looking at things. It's one of the biggest joys in my life, or maybe "calming" is a better word for it. Looking at things is the best source of inspiration. Clothes, buildings, ugly handbags, beautiful chairs, the supermarket, the way someone is dressed on the TTC…

I want to be a Gonzo journalist (my sincerest apologies, this post has officially gone all over the place)

I want to look at the object, the person buying the object, the person selling the object, the person designing the object, and then follow the money up and up and up.

And then tie it all to capitalism.

We're sold the fantasy of scarcity, the fantasy of craftsmanship, the fantasy of Paris, the fantasy of Italy, the fantasy of the atelier, the fantasy of being the kind of person who owns the thing.

And that is where the designer houses get richer, the consumer gets dumber, and I apparently get a blog post out of it.

Azal BASBOUS💜

items.title: Sugar-Free Fries & Other Lies
items.summary: STOP PROMOTING UR SUGAR-FREE FRIES AND KETO YOGURTS. The wellness craze in…
items.content_html:
STOP PROMOTING UR SUGAR-FREE FRIES AND KETO YOGURTS.

The wellness craze in Lebanon is out of control. Around summer 2024 with an absolute PEAK in spring 2025, collagen smoothie places and random pilates studios hatched at every street corner of Beirut.

I am not talking about Backburner; that place was always around, even if it turned into an overpriced "to-be-seen" hub overnight. I mean places like The Glow Paradise. There are dozens like it now, but it's their toxic marketing feeding young girls lies about wellness that specifically pisses me. 

I won't even question their ingredient quality. At those prices, I pray to GOD it's top tier (though I’d love to know the actual farm names for this supposed local "grass-fed beef" in Lebanon, because IT IS THOSE farmers who deserve real recognition after the crisis). No, what gets me is the 3-digit label right next to every marvelously named food item on their menu: the calorie count.

How MANY TIMES have I stumbled on videos of influencers my age trying the Glow matcha that "only has 120 kcal guys"!!!!! It exasperates me.

One, because these influencers usually have absolutely no clue what the hell they are talking about. They scan their meals every day with an AI calorie counter app, then complain to their followers about having a crumb of sponge cake.

I am not attacking those influencers. But as someone who has suffered with an eating disorder, I can't sit and watch people PROMOTING that kind of stuff to others. If someone is struggling, I hope from the bottom of my heart that they have the support they need, but please save that for tumblr thinspo and not the FYP of a random tween who has never even heard of calories before.

Also, it is incredibly interesting that "healthful" foods are systematically marketed to women. Look at The Glow Paradise's posts: women in bikinis or tight little Alo Yoga sets posing with a "protein papa" juice. It’s alarming how seamlessly Western activewear branding is pushing Eurocentric body standards onto Arab women. Or simply look at the captions: "youthful face," "rejuvenation," "game changer for skin health"... They are selling anti-aging to a clientele made of teens and young adults.

Helloo???? What about ESSENTIAL health?

It blows my mind how our society continuously mistakes a woman’s physical appearance for actual "health" instead of her internal organ function.

Obviously one follows the other: if your body is operating right internally, the rest shows. But when young girls end up chronically undereating because they are terrified of calories, believe me it will completely wreck their fertility, bone density, and actual hair health. No amount of collagen powder saves your endocrine system when you are running a massive calorie deficit lol.

Posting those HYPER-curated bodies sets impossibly toxic expectations, especially for Arab girls. I am not generalizing, but from actual experience, observation, and like basic scientific facts, Arab female physiognomy (fat distribution, bone structures…) is BIOLOGICALLY, different from that of ultra-lean Western French sticks!

To make matters worse, they are hypocritically flooding their Insta feed with words like "nourish, nourish, nourish." Like they even have weight loss plans. I have no clue how they interact with their clients, but I really hope they inform them properly instead of throwing them into a giant orthorexia pit.

(Uhm, so side note: I realized I keep saying "they." When I say "they," I mean The Glow Paradise. But let's be real this predatory pattern exists everywhere in the world, not just Beirut)

ALSO, I am not saying people should be completely oblivious to the energetic values of what they ingest! I would be a crazy person and healthcare worker if I discouraged basic nutritional literacy. Take the US or Canada, if there was no nutritional info on menus, people would spend their whole daily energy expenditure on one peameal bacon bagel. So we need to educate people in a realistic and scientific way!

Yes, whole foods are best for our bodies. Yes, everything is processed nowadays. But surprise surprise, whole foods today are ALSO processed. So when you spend $11 on four pieces of organic chicken nuggets, each the size of my thumb, or a sad little omelette, you are 1. wasting money and 2. missing the actual experience of going out to eat. You can make all of that at home for a quarter of the price. Stop being so gullible to aesthetic pastel colored pretty plates and the vibe of a place just to avoid looking at what you are actually ingesting. (If you want an example of a spot actually doing healthful food right, look at places like Honest Greens).

The best thing in my and EXPERTS' opinion (it should be standard advice, really) is to eat healthy at home. And by HEALTHY, I mean eat the rainbow, avoid processed dairy products or heavy store-bought dressings, ditch the zero-sugar carbonated drinks (the chemical additives damage ur gut microbiome)… Then, when you TREAT yourself by going out, have something you CANNOT cook at home. We have normalized eating out so much today when it used to be a luxury!

All this to say: before getting sucked into the goop-flavored black hole of wellness aesthetic, please educate yourself, and please please please be careful with what you consume online. If you are ever in need of support, please reach out to your loved ones. I never want anyone to feel like they aren't good enough. Love yourself and be kind to others.

items.title: La Gazelle de Waller
items.summary: Imaginez la personne la plus chic, la plus discrète et la plus…
items.content_html:
Imaginez la personne la plus chic, la plus discrète et la plus cultivée que vous puissiez croiser : c'est exactement ce que j'appelle une Gazelle de Waller. J'ai tenu à ce que ma toute première publication ici soit consacrée à ce concept parce qu'il me semble indispensable que mes lecteurs et lectrices observent le monde à travers cette grille de lecture, ne serait-ce que pour saisir le fil conducteur de mes prochains posts.

Bon, retour à notre sujet. Une Gazelle de Waller, c’est quelqu’un qui n’a absolument rien à prouver (when ykyk). C'est le produit d'un confort générationnel familial qui dépasse les simples critères financiers "d'aisance". Elle doit venir d'une famille éduquée respectable qui a de bonnes valeurs et toujours attachée à ses traditions.

Chez la Gazelle de Waller, le luxe n'a rien d'ostentatoire. Puisque, justement, elle a grandi dans un environnement raffiné, pour elle, c'est tout à fait normal d'être entourée de ce qu'il y'a de mieux. Alors quand je parle de luxe, je ne fais évidemment PAS référence aux it-bags de la saison, à la logomania ou à tout ce qui crie sa marque à dix mètres (l'horreur absolue). Je fais plutôt référence à choisir systématiquement ce qu’il y a de plus noble comme matière sans jamais opter pour ce qui est facilement identifiable (qu'il s'agisse d'un cuir de veau Box pleine fleur, d'une pure vigogne, ou d'une soie grège brute). Bref, le savoir-faire et la durabilité priment sur tout le reste.

Cette même exigence se retrouve dans son rapport aux autres. La bienséance et l'étiquette chez la Gazelle de Waller sont instinctivement intégrées. Elle sait où aller, comment se comporter, quoi dire, quand se taire. On peut aussi bien la croiser emmitouflée dans un manteau vintage seconde-main au lobby d'un grand hôtel parisien qu'attablée le lendemain sur un tabouret en plastique au cœur d'une médina, un thé à la menthe à la main. Tout cela bien évidemment sans perdre sa confiance et sa noblesse. 

Son érudition ferait pâlir les théories de Bourdieu sur le capital culturel : elle comprend l'art, la haute parfumerie, la gastronomie, les matières et la littérature... Même en voyage, la quête d'authenticité prend le dessus sur les adresses trendy de la saison. Elle préfère une petite table dénichée au coin d'une ruelle plutôt qu'un resto où tout le monde se presse et fait la queue.

Dans son univers discret (qu'il ne faudrait SURTOUT pas le confondre avec de l'hésitation ou de la timidité) chaque détail autour d'elle est minutieusement observé. On pourrait facilement passer à côté d'une Gazelle de Waller sur le trottoir sans y prêter attention, mais pour quiconque sait vraiment observer, sa présence finit toujours par triompher.

P.S. Pourquoi ce nom ? Parce que la Gazelle de Waller  (aussi connu sous le nom de Gérénuk) est sans doute l'animal rare le plus absurdement élégant de la savane, ne vivant qu'en très petit groupe. Considérez désormais ce blog comme leur point de ralliement.

P.S. 2 : La vraie Gazelle de Waller, c'est ma Mima (et ses sœurs).

items.title: Helloes, to the Habibis
items.summary: Alors. This "blog" (or whatever you want to call it) is entirely…
items.content_html:
Alors.
 
This "blog" (or whatever you want to call it) is entirely dedicated to my opinion. So if you continue reading this, you will probably notice that my brain doesn't really know how to turn off.
 
I spend a ridiculous amount of time getting interested in things that technically have no link whatsoever to my career-in-the-making. I am a full-time undergrad studen set on studying medicine… but there is nothing more deplorable to me than a doctor with zero cultural capital.
 
And so I collect a bit of knowledge from everything: magazines (Monocle, Rest of World, 1Granary, Vestoj, Cereal…), anything written by Nora Ephron (my literary queen), random podcasts, Enquête exclusive documentaries, Arte YouTube videos...
 
Bref, it provides me with a good break from the apical and basal domains of epithelial cells.
 
I will skip the details, but my bottom line is that undergrad pre-med students need to get their heads of cells and see the world as a WHOLE, not just as proteins and lipids. See the social aspect: how people think and what they like. Discover different niches. Detach themselves a bit from the quite toxic, dare I say, scientific community. It gives their brains a break, and it just makes life a lot more interesting.
 
I have my notebooks; I take them everywhere. I used to get the Legami ones from Fnac, but I recently upgraded to a Moleskine for the first time (very Gazelle de Waller).
 
I never leave without one. If you say stuff in class like "branching out from that" or even "that concludes my presentation, thank you," I’M WRITING THAT DOWN. If I go to a restaurant and the menu says "smoked trout rillettes," I'm also writing that down. So, in less than a year, I fell down the rabbit hole of the design behind IKEA’s winding paths, consumerism, CAN Ibiza, the disappearance of newsstands on Toronto sidewalks, hotel concierges (Mr. Gustave, my icon), organic toilet paper, Hermès Horizons...
 
Basically, I'll use all of this in my posts. I have long been thinking about how hard it is to think alone sometimes, so I am seeking a community of like-minded people. Not in an elitist way, but in the spirit of Bourdieu’s cultural capital. I want to have this community where everyone is curious. And together, we will enrich our cultural capital.
 
Obviously, this should to be a two-way street. I will enable the comment section under every single post because my goal is to exchange knowledge. I want to learn from my readers just as much as I share what’s in my notebooks. Tell me what I missed, challenge my assumptions... give me new info, idk.
 
I know this sounds all over the place. I'll get better at writing, don't worry lol.
 
So consider this an "evolving" guide on how to get the cultural capital of a Gazelle de Waller.
 
Read along. Or don't, habibi.
